word:greek-nt:G0028.explanation: Hagar is a personal name, referring to the woman named Hagar. In the Greek New Testament, it appears twice, both times in Galatians 4:24–25. As a name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is primarily its identification of a particular person. The surrounding passage determines what is being said about Hagar in each occurrence; the name itself does not carry an additional ordinary definition beyond identifying her.

word:greek-nt:G0077.explanation: This word means “free” or “free of charge,” describing something provided without requiring payment. It functions as an adjective, identifying what is offered without cost rather than something purchased or owed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 9:18. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is clear: something is given or done without charge. The word therefore emphasizes the absence of financial cost.

word:greek-nt:G0095.explanation: “Unjustly” describes an action carried out in a way that is not just or fair. It functions as an adverb, telling how something is done rather than naming a person, object, or event. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, at 1 Peter 2:19. Its basic meaning focuses on the manner of an action: the action is performed unjustly. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain what action is being described there.

word:greek-nt:G0154.explanation: Aiteō means to ask or request. It can also refer to petitioning for something, or to a forceful demand.

word:greek-nt:G0271.explanation: Amethustos means amethyst, a kind of rock crystal.

word:greek-nt:G0352.explanation: Anakypto means to raise oneself or look up. It can also describe straightening oneself up from a bent position.

word:greek-nt:G0460.explanation: This word means “without law.” It describes someone or something considered outside the condition of being governed by law. As a negative expression, it emphasizes the absence of law rather than naming a particular kind of law or explaining why it is absent. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both within one verse in Romans, so its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:greek-nt:G0565.explanation: Aperchomai means to go away or depart.

word:greek-nt:G0587.explanation: Apodektos means acceptable, welcome, or pleasing—something received favorably.

word:greek-nt:G0604.explanation: Apokatallassō means to reconcile—to change from one state of feeling to another.

word:greek-nt:G0749.explanation: Archiereus means high priest or chief priest.

word:greek-nt:G0851.explanation: Aphaireō means to take away or remove. It can also mean to strike something off, as when an ear is cut off.

word:greek-nt:G0903.explanation: Balaam is a personal name, referring to the son of Beor.

word:greek-nt:G0976.explanation: Biblos means a written book or volume.

word:greek-nt:G1140.explanation: Daimonion means an evil spirit or demon. It can also refer to a heathen deity.

word:greek-nt:G1386.explanation: This word means “deceitful”: it describes someone or something that uses deception rather than acting openly and honestly. It points to a lack of straightforwardness and to conduct intended to mislead. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 11:13. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the character or practice of deception.

word:greek-nt:G1401.explanation: Doulos means an enslaved person or male slave, serving under another’s authority. It may be rendered servant when the person is expected to carry out another’s commands.

word:greek-nt:G1557.explanation: Ekdikēsis means avenging, vindication, or vengeance. It may describe avenging an oppressed person or bringing punishment on those who do not obey.

word:greek-nt:G1610.explanation: Ekrizō means to root out or uproot.

word:greek-nt:G1746.explanation: Endyo means to put on clothing or to clothe someone else.

word:greek-nt:G1939.explanation: Epithumia means desire or eagerness for something. It can describe a strong longing, such as a desire to depart or to see someone, and it can also mean an inordinate desire or lust, including fleshly or youthful lusts.

word:greek-nt:G2044.explanation: Ereugomai means to utter or declare.

word:greek-nt:G2116.explanation: Euthunō means to make a way straight in its direction. It can also mean to guide or steer.

word:greek-nt:G2163.explanation: Euphemos means admirable or commendable, describing what is of good report.

word:greek-nt:G2325.explanation: Therizō means to reap, as when one person sows and another reaps.

word:greek-nt:G2398.explanation: Idios means one's own or belonging to a person. It can also describe something private.

word:greek-nt:G2475.explanation: Israelite means a person belonging to the people of Israel. Scripture connects Israelites with the covenants, the giving of the law, service, and promises.

word:greek-nt:G2497.explanation: Jorim is a personal name. In the Greek New Testament, it refers to a person named in the genealogy recorded in Luke. The name occurs one time, in Luke 3:29, and the English rendering preserves it as “Jorim.” Because no verse text or surrounding context is provided here, the name itself does not support adding details about this person’s character, role, or significance. Its basic function is simply to identify one individual within Luke’s genealogical record.

word:greek-nt:G2541.explanation: Kaisar means Caesar, a name used for the emperor.

word:greek-nt:G2642.explanation: This Greek verb means “to stone” or “to stone to death,” describing the act of killing someone by throwing stones at them. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 20:6. The precise force of the word in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and conversation, but its basic meaning is the deliberate use of stoning as a means of execution.

word:greek-nt:G2707.explanation: Kataphronetēs means a despiser or scoffer.

word:greek-nt:G2758.explanation: Kenoo means to empty. It can also mean to deprive something of its content, making it void or of no effect.

word:greek-nt:G2800.explanation: This word means “breaking,” referring plainly to the act or process of breaking something. It appears twice in the Greek New Testament, once in Luke 24:35 and once in Acts 2:42. The same basic meaning is represented in both occurrences. The surrounding verse and passage determine exactly what is being broken or how the action functions there, but the word itself centers on breaking rather than on a broader spiritual or doctrinal idea.

word:greek-nt:G2934.explanation: Ktenos means an animal. It can refer to an animal used for riding.

word:greek-nt:G2981.explanation: This Greek New Testament word means “speech”—the act or content of speaking. It refers to words expressed aloud rather than to a person, place, or abstract quality. In the New Testament, it occurs three times, all in three separate verses: once in Matthew and twice in John. Its ordinary sense remains focused on spoken language, while the surrounding verse determines whose speech is meant and what significance those words have in that passage.

word:greek-nt:G3061.explanation: Loimos means pestilence. It can also describe a pestilent fellow.

word:greek-nt:G3115.explanation: Makrothumia means patience, forbearance, or longsuffering.

word:greek-nt:G3379.explanation: Mēpote means lest, marking a possible outcome to be avoided. It can also mean whether perhaps, expressing uncertainty about an alternative.

word:greek-nt:G3414.explanation: Mna means a mina, a Greek monetary unit equal to 100 drachma.

word:greek-nt:G3537.explanation: This word means a “basin for washing” or “wash basin”—a container used to hold water for washing. It names the vessel itself, not the act of washing or the water. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in John 13:5. Since the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s specific role in that scene is not expanded beyond its ordinary meaning as a washing basin.

word:greek-nt:G3568.explanation: Nyn means now, referring to the present time.

word:greek-nt:G3623.explanation: Oikonomos means a household manager or steward. One example shows a manager overseeing another person’s possessions, while another places a steward over a household to distribute food at the proper time.

word:greek-nt:G3656.explanation: Homileō means to converse or talk with others. It can also describe associating or keeping company with others.

word:greek-nt:G3784.explanation: Opheilo means to owe. It can also express what someone ought to do.

word:greek-nt:G3847.explanation: Parabasis means transgression. It is used where law is in view, and Adam’s transgression is one example of its use.

word:greek-nt:G3902.explanation: Parasēmos can refer to a ship’s figurehead.

word:greek-nt:G4037.explanation: This word means “to await” or “to wait for,” describing the act of remaining in expectation of someone or something. It presents waiting as deliberate attention directed toward what is expected, rather than merely passing time. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 1:4. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the patient act of waiting for what has been promised or anticipated.

word:greek-nt:G4068.explanation: This word means “to boast”: to speak proudly about oneself or one’s achievements. It functions as a verb, describing an act of proud self-expression rather than simply possessing a good quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Corinthians 13:4. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, which are needed to show exactly how this boasting is being described.

word:greek-nt:G4114.explanation: Platos means breadth or width, a dimension measured alongside length and height when describing the size of something.

word:greek-nt:G4284.explanation: This word means “to be better off” or “to excel.” It describes having an advantage or standing above others in some respect. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Romans 3:9, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word itself expresses comparison: one person or group is regarded as better positioned, superior, or advantaged rather than merely existing or acting. [evidence IDs: p03:word:greek-nt:G4284:identity, p03:word:greek-nt:G4284:occurrences]

word:greek-nt:G4323.explanation: Prosanatithemi means to consult with or confer. It can also mean to impart or add something.

word:greek-nt:G4415.explanation: Prōtotokia means birthright—the rights of the firstborn.

word:greek-nt:G4561.explanation: Sarx means flesh. It can refer to physical flesh, describe human nature as sinful flesh, or identify human relatives according to the flesh.

word:greek-nt:G4693.explanation: Spēlaion means a cave, den, or hideout.

word:greek-nt:G4806.explanation: This word means “to make alive with,” describing the act of bringing someone or something to life together with another. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person, place, or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Ephesians 2:5 and Colossians 2:13. Its precise force in either verse is understood more fully from the surrounding sentence and passage.

word:greek-nt:G4873.explanation: Synanakeimai means to recline at table with others—to dine or eat with them.

word:greek-nt:G4899.explanation: This word means “chosen together with” or “chosen with,” describing someone selected alongside another person or group. It expresses shared choosing rather than selection in isolation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, at 1 Peter 5:13, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. The word’s central idea remains association through being chosen together with someone else, not merely being present with them. This is a lexical description, while the verse context determines whom it identifies and why that designation matters.

word:greek-nt:G4950.explanation: Syrtis is a proper name for a geographical place. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 27:17, and functions as a place-name rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name itself identifies the location; understanding its specific setting requires the surrounding verse and passage. Its meaning is therefore primarily the name of the place itself, not an abstract idea or personal quality.

word:greek-nt:G5045.explanation: Tekton means a carpenter. It can also mean an artisan.

word:greek-nt:G5180.explanation: Typtō means to beat or strike. It describes a physical blow, such as striking someone on the head with a reed.

word:greek-nt:G5203.explanation: This word describes someone suffering from edema, also called dropsy—a condition involving abnormal swelling from retained fluid. It functions as a descriptive word for a person affected by that illness, rather than naming a general feeling of discomfort or suffering. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 14:2, and its meaning is specifically tied to this bodily condition. The word therefore identifies a person by a visible medical disorder, while the surrounding verse supplies the fuller setting.

word:greek-nt:G5276.explanation: This word refers to a “pit for a winepress” or a “trough”—the place or container where juice from pressed grapes was gathered. It is a concrete noun describing part of a winepress, not the act of pressing itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 12:1, within Jesus’ description of a vineyard’s preparation. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain its particular role in that passage.

word:greek-nt:G5351.explanation: Phtheirō means to corrupt or destroy.

word:greek-nt:G5430.explanation: Phronimōs means wisely, sensibly, or prudently. In the passage, it describes the dishonest manager’s shrewd action, showing practical wisdom without calling him honest.

word:greek-nt:G5492.explanation: This word describes being storm-tossed—being battered and driven about by a storm. It portrays a person or vessel caught in severe, disturbing weather rather than moving calmly or under control. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:18. The word itself names the storm-battered condition; the precise force of the statement in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:greek-nt:G5553.explanation: Chrysion means gold, including a piece of gold or a golden ornament.
